ENG 501
                      Short Notes Lecture (23-45)
Definitions
Arbitrariness In human language, there is no natural connection between the word and the
:             object they make reference to. This characteristic of language is called
              arbitrariness. For example, the Arabic word ‘kalab’ meaning dog and the English
              word ‘dog’ have no relation to the word they refer to.

Bow Wow       In English= splash, bang, boom, rattle, buzz, hiss, screech, bow-wow Also called
theory :      the “bow-wow theory” of language origin

Conservative It means that tends to preserve the existing status.
:

Creole :      A creole language is a stable language that originated from a pidgin language, but
              has since been “nativized” (i.e. taught to, and acquired by, children). Its
              vocabulary is based on that of a parent language, although usually with significant
              pronunciation, meaning and grammar differences.

Derivation : Derivation creates new words with different meanings, e.g. maltreat from treat.
             With different syntactic properties, e.g. the adverb quickly from the adjective
             quick.

Diachronic Diachronic linguistics (or historical linguistics), the study of a language over a
linguistics : period of time.

Dialect :     A dialect is a variety or version of a language spoken in a particular geographical
              area. Different dialects are distinguished from each other by their vocabulary,
              grammar and pronunciation (whereas a distinction made only in terms of
              pronunciation is usually called an accent). A dialect of a language is
              distinguishable, but still understandable, to speakers of another dialect of that
              language.

Displacement In linguistics, displacement is the capability of language to communicate about
:            things that are not immediately present (spatially or temporally); i.e., things that
             are either not here or are not here now.

Duality :     Human language is organized at two levels or layers simultaneously. We have a
              physical level at which we can produce individual sounds, like n, b and i. As
              individual sounds, none of these discrete forms has any intrinsic meaning. In a

               particular combination such as bin, we have another level producing a meaning
               that is different from the meaning of the combination in nib.Among other
               creatures, each communicative signal appears to be a single fixed form that cannot
               be broken down into separate parts.Your dog may be able to produce woof (“I’m
               happy to see you”).It does not seem to do so on the basis of a distinct level of
               production combining the separate elements of w+oo+f. If the dog was operating
               with the double level (i.e. duality), then we might expect to hear different
               combinations with different meanings, such as oowf (“I’m hungry”) and foow
               (“I’m really bored”).

Englishes :    World English is one language and Englishes are different variety of English like
               Austrian English, American English and South Asian English (Indian English,
               Pakistan English etc.)

Family tree First attempt at depicting the relationships between languages. Has assumptions:
model :     The Regularity Hypothesis The Relatedness Hypothesis

Inflection :   Inflection deals with patterns of word structure that are determined by the role of
               words in sentences. For example, a pronoun like he has the forms he, him and his
               depending on whether it is subject, object or possessive in a given sentence.

Juncture :     The pauses or connections between words, phrases, and sentences.

Linguistics : Linguistics is the scientific study of language.

Long vowels The "long" vowels are: • "a" as in "paper", • "e" as in "be", • "u" as in "human".
:

Morphology In linguistics, Morphology is the study of words, how they are formed, and their
:          relationship to other words in the same language. It analyzes the structure of
           words and parts of words, such as stems, root words, prefixes, and suffixes.

Neolithic      “Neolithic” is likewise a convenient rather than scientific term. They possessed a
age :          superior kind of stone implement, and generally a higher culture. It was a dark
               race of slightly larger stature than the Paleolithic population.

Orthography An orthography is a set of conventions for writing a language. It includes norms
:           of spelling, hyphenation, capitalization, word breaks, emphasis, and punctuation.

Phonology      Phonology is the study of how sounds are organized and used in natural
of a           languages. It is the study of different sounds and the way they come together to
language :     form speech and words - such as the comparison of the sounds of the two "p"
               sounds in "pop-up."

Pitch :        Pitch – how high or low a voice is when producing a sound

Renaissance Renaissance was a time of “revival of learning,” records of Greek civilization
:           became once more available. Latin and Greek were the key to the world’s
            knowledge and were highly esteemed for poetry, oratory, and philosophy.

Reverse     Reverse Loanwords are words from other languages into English. It is a reverse
Loanwords : adoption process in which words from languages are brought into English.
            Examples: Stop, sport, tennis, golf, weekend, jeans, bar, airport, hotel, etc., are
            among the most universally used in the world.

Short vowel Short vowel are: • "a" as in "cat", • "e" as in "red",
:

Standard      Standard English is whatever form of the English language is accepted (at any
English :     point in time, and in any particular country) as the national norm, encompassing

Spread of English in South Asia?
The worldwide spread of English is an unprecedented phenomenon for which we do not find any example in
human history. English was brought to the subcontinent in the early seventeenth century by British colonialism.
Today, it is spoken as a second language by 3 percent of the population of Bangladesh, Bhutan, India, the
Maldives, Nepal, Pakistan, and Sri Lanka. In numerical terms, we can safely say that there are approximately 33
million English speaking people.
South Asian English is sometimes called ‘Indian English’ as British India included most of the region, but
today, the varieties of English are usually divided according to the modern states. In India, there are 25 million
users of English, even more than Australia. There are intra-national and intra-regional role of ‘link’ language
among people of diverse linguistic backgrounds. After so many years of independence, the countries of South
Asia still use English to varying degrees in the domains of government administration, law, the military, higher
education, commerce, the media, and the arts.
In Pakistan, English has the status of an official language alongside the national language, Urdu. In Sri Lanka,
there are efforts to ‘peoplize’ English. In Bangladesh, despite strong Bangla movement, English enjoys
importance. In South Asian countries, it plays the role of the international medium for communication with the
global community of nations.
Features of South Asian English
Indian English
It has words of Indian vernaculars that have made their way into the English language.
Examples include jungle, tank, bungalow, shampoo, verandah.
It has political, sociological, and administrative terms of modern India: dharna, hartal, eveteasing, votebank,
swdeshi, tiffin, hillstation, gymkhana. We need to notice its resemblance with Pakistani English.
Vocabulary
•      Our company lays great stress on technical training and knowledge ‘upgradation’.
•      The Prime Minister greeted the presspersons with a ‘namaskar’ and a broad smile.
•      I read the newspaper ‘matrimonials’ on Sundays, especially the ‘English-knowing’ intelligentsia.
Spelling and Pronunciation
Most Indian languages, unlike English, have a nearly phonetic spelling, so the spelling of a word is a highly
reliable guide to its pronunciation. The word ‘of’ is usually pronounced with a /f/ instead of a /v/ as in most

other accents. Pronunciation of <house> as [hauz] is prevalent for both noun and verb instead of [haus] as noun
and [hauz] as verb.

What was swift’s proposal?
       By the beginning of the eighteenth century, grounds had been prepared and time was ripe for an
authoritative plan for an academy. With the example of Richelieu and the French Academy, doubtless in his
mind, Swift addressed a letter in 1712 to the earl of Oxford, Lord Treasurer of England. It was published under
the title A Proposal for Correcting, Improving, and Ascertaining the English Tongue. After the usual
formalities, he then launches an attack against the innovations he had objected to in his paper, the Tatler, two
years before. The remedy he offered was that a free sensible choice should be made of such persons, as are
generally allowed to be best qualified for such a work, without any regard to quality, party, or profession. …
‘These, to a certain number at least, should assemble at some appointed time and place, and fix on rules, by
which they design to proceed. What methods they will take, is not for me to prescribe.’ The work of this group,
as he conceives it, is described in the following terms:
‘The persons who are to undertake this work will have the example of the French before them to imitate, where
these have proceeded right, and to avoid their mistakes.’ He further added:
‘… Besides the grammar-part, wherein we are allowed to be very defective, they will observe many gross
improprieties, which, however authorized by practice, and grown familiar, ought to be discarded. They will find
many words that deserve to be utterly thrown out of our language, many more to be corrected, and perhaps not a
few long since antiquated, which ought to be restored on account of their energy and sound.’
       The publication of Swift’s Proposal marks the culmination of the movement for an English Academy.
Swift’s proposal was objected and opposed by several people, mainly on political grounds. Swift’s proposal was
not followed up properly and no serious effort was made to accomplish the purpose.
Progressive passive?
The extension of such forms to the passive (the house is being built) was a later development. It belongs to the
very end of the eighteenth century. Old English had no progressive passive. Such an expression as the man is
loved, feared, hated is progressive only in so far as the verbs loving, fearing, hating imply a continuous state.

Q. What is Black Death? (Topic 75)
This event is known in the history as ‘The Black Death’. It was in the summer of 1348 that in the
Southwest of England, first case of this plague was reported. These were the first cases of a disease
that in its contagiousness and fatality exceeded anything previously known. The Black Death
spread rapidly over the rest of the country, reaching its height in 1349.40 percent of the parish
clergy died of the plague. Death rate during the plague approximated 30 percent. The effects of so
great a calamity were naturally serious. Mortality was greatest among the lower social orders. The
question arises why mortality was greatest among the lower social orders? The answer is simple:
it happened because their life style was poor, hygiene conditions were bad and affordability to
medicine was very low. The result of these deaths was a labor shortage which consequently gave
rise to increase in wages.
Q. Chaucer short vowels a and u (Topic 101)
   ❖ If we compare Chaucer’s pronunciation of the short vowels with ours, we note only two
     changes of importance, those of a and u.
   ❖ In some cases this ME a represented an OE æ (at, apple, back), and the new pronunciation
     was therefore a return to approximately the form that the word had had in Old English.
   ❖ In Chaucer’s pronunciation these had still their so-called “continental” value—that is, a
     was pronounced like the a in father and not as in name. Also in Chaucer’s pronunciation e
     was either like the e in there or the a in mate, but not like the eei n meet.
Q. What’s the Great Vowel Shift? (Topic 102)
The situation is very different when we consider the long vowels. In Chaucer’s pronunciation,
these had still their so-called ‘continental’ value—that is, a was pronounced like the ain father and
not as in name. Also in Chaucer’s pronunciation e was either like the e in there or the ain mate,
but not like the eein meet. But in 15th century, a great change happened i.e. all the long vowels
gradually came to be pronounced with a greater elevation of the tongue and closing of the mouth.
Most of the long vowels had approximately acquired their present pronunciation at least by the
sixteenth century. The change occurred at the end of the seventeenth century and had become
general by the middle of the eighteenth. The spelling of English had become fixed in a general
way before the shift and therefore did not change when the quality of the long vowels changed.
Consequently, our vowel symbols no longer correspond to the sounds they once represented in
English and still represent in the other modern languages.

Q. Varieties of English in South Asia
  • Bangladeshi English
  •     Indian English
  •     Nepali English
  •     Pakistani English
  •     Sri Lankan English
  Q. Spread of English in South Asia?

  The worldwide spread of English is an unprecedented phenomenon for which we do not find any example in

  human history. English was brought to the subcontinent in the early seventeenth century by British

  colonialism. Today, it is spoken as a second language by 3 percent of the population of Bangladesh, Bhutan,

  India, the Maldives, Nepal, Pakistan, and Sri Lanka. In numerical terms, we can safely say that there are

  approximately 33 million English speaking people.

  South Asian English is sometimes called ‘Indian English’ as British India included most of the region, but

  today, the varieties of English are usually divided according to the modern states. In India, there are 25 million

  users of English, even more than Australia. There are intra-national and intra-regional role of ‘link’ language

  among people of diverse linguistic backgrounds. After so many years of independence, the countries of South

  Asia still use English to varying degrees in the domains of government administration, law, the military, higher

  education, commerce, the media, and the arts.

  In Pakistan, English has the status of an official language alongside the national language, Urdu. In Sri Lanka,

  there are efforts to ‘peoplize’ English. In Bangladesh, despite strong Bangla movement, English enjoys

  importance. In South Asian countries, it plays the role of the international medium for communication with

  the global community of nations.

Q. "To be forms" (3)

It is impossible to follow the subject matter here in extensive details so only significant ones can be pointed out. One
characteristic development in English grammar in the eighteenth century is regarding progressive verb forms.

        Where French Says: je chante or German ich singe

MAHA MALIK’S COMPILATION                                                                                        Page 2

Do-forms are emphatic forms. But their most important uses are in negative and interrogative sentences (I don’t
sing, do you sing?). To be formsand the present participle are generally called progressive forms. Their most
common use is to indicate an action as being in progress at the time implied by the auxiliary. The wide extension of
the use of progressive forms is one of the most important developments of the English verb in the modern period. In
Old English, such expressions as ‘he woes lærende’ (he was teaching) are occasionally found but usually in
translations from Latin. In early Middle English, progressive forms are distinctly rare. Their number increases in the
Middle English period and the credit of their development goes to the sixteenth century. The chief factor in their
growth is the use of the participle as a noun governed by the preposition on (he burst out on laughing). This
weakened to he burst out a-laughing and finally to he burst out laughing. In the same way he was on laughing
became he was a-laughing and he was laughing. Today such forms are freely used in all tenses (is laughing, was
laughing, will be laughing, etc.).

Q. What was swift’s proposal?
       By the beginning of the eighteenth century, grounds had been prepared and time was ripe for an
authoritative plan for an academy. With the example of Richelieu and the French Academy, doubtless in his
mind, Swift addressed a letter in 1712 to the earl of Oxford, Lord Treasurer of England. It was published under
the title A Proposal for Correcting, Improving, and Ascertaining the English Tongue. After the usual
formalities, he then launches an attack against the innovations he had objected to in his paper, the Tatler, two
years before. The remedy he offered was that a free sensible choice should be made of such persons, as are
generally allowed to be best qualified for such a work, without any regard to quality, party, or profession. …
‘These, to a certain number at least, should assemble at some appointed time and place, and fix on rules, by
which they design to proceed. What methods they will take, is not for me to prescribe.’ The work of this group,
as he conceives it, is described in the following terms:
‘The persons who are to undertake this work will have the example of the French before them to imitate, where
these have proceeded right, and to avoid their mistakes.’ He further added:
‘… Besides the grammar-part, wherein we are allowed to be very defective, they will observe many gross
improprieties, which, however authorized by practice, and grown familiar, ought to be discarded. They will find
many words that deserve to be utterly thrown out of our language, many more to be corrected, and perhaps not a
few long since antiquated, which ought to be restored on account of their energy and sound.’
       The publication of Swift’s Proposal marks the culmination of the movement for an English Academy.
Swift’s proposal was objected and opposed by several people, mainly on political grounds. Swift’s proposal was
not followed up properly and no serious effort was made to accomplish the purpose.

Q. What is Black Death? (Topic 75)

This event is known in the history as ‘The Black Death’. It was in the summer of
1348 that in the Southwest of England, first case of this plague was reported. These
were the first cases of a disease that in its contagiousness and fatality exceeded
anything previously known. The Black Death spread rapidly over the rest of the
country, reaching its height in 1349.40 percent of the parish clergy died of the
plague. Death rate during the plague approximated 30 percent. The effects of so
great a calamity were naturally serious. Mortality was greatest among the lower
social orders. The question arises why mortality was greatest among the lower
social orders? The answer is simple: it happened because their life style was poor,
hygiene conditions were bad and affordability to medicine was very low. The
result of these deaths was a labor shortage which consequently gave rise to
increase in wages.

       pronunciation was therefore a return to approximately the form that the word
       had had in Old English.
       In Chaucer’s pronunciation these had still their so-called “continental”

Q. What’s the Great Vowel Shift? (Topic 102)

Maha Malik’s Compilation                                                      Page 1

The situation is very different when we consider the long vowels. In Chaucer’s
pronunciation, these had still their so-called ‘continental’ value—that is, a was
pronounced like the ain father and not as in name. Also in Chaucer’s pronunciation
e was either like the e in there or the ain mate, but not like the eein meet. But in
15th century, a great change happened i.e. all the long vowels gradually came to be
pronounced with a greater elevation of the tongue and closing of the mouth. Most
of the long vowels had approximately acquired their present pronunciation at least
by the sixteenth century. The change occurred at the end of the seventeenth century
and had become general by the middle of the eighteenth. The spelling of English
had become fixed in a general way before the shift and therefore did not change
when the quality of the long vowels changed. Consequently, our vowel symbols no
longer correspond to the sounds they once represented in English and still
represent in the other modern languages.

Question ❓

Many words in the English language are spelled phonetically, but some are spelled according to orthographic rules that are not so intuitive. The only way to understand the anomalies of spelling is to study the history of language.

Solution

Yes, studying the history of the English language is crucial for understanding the anomalies of spelling. English spelling is a complex system that has evolved over centuries, influenced by various languages, cultural shifts, and scribal practices. To grasp the inconsistencies and irregularities in spelling, it's essential to delve into the language's history.

*The Evolving Nature of English Spelling*

English spelling is not a straightforward reflection of pronunciation. It reflects the language's historical development, incorporating influences from Old English, Latin, French, and other languages. Over time, pronunciation has changed, while spelling has largely remained fixed, leading to inconsistencies between the two.

*Examples of Historical Influences on Spelling*

* *Old English Influence:* The word "through" is pronounced with the same vowel sound as "though" due to the Great Vowel Shift, which occurred between the 15th and 17th centuries. However, the spelling remains distinct, reflecting the Old English forms "þurh" and "þeáh."

* *Latin Influence:* The word "knight" is pronounced with the same consonant sound as "night" due to Norman French influence. The "k" in "knight" reflects the Latin spelling "cniht," while the "gh" in "night" represents the Old English pronunciation.

*The Role of Scribes and Printers*

Scribes and printers have also played a role in shaping English spelling. They often introduced their own idiosyncratic spellings, which sometimes became widely adopted. This further contributed to the inconsistencies in the language's spelling system.

*Understanding Anomalies through Historical Context*

Studying the history of English spelling provides context for understanding the anomalies. By examining the language's evolution and the influences that have shaped it, we can better appreciate the complexities of the spelling system and the reasons behind its irregularities.

*Conclusion*

While English spelling may appear perplexing at times, delving into the language's history can shed light on the reasons behind its anomalies. By understanding the historical context and the various factors that have influenced spelling, we can gain a deeper appreciation for the richness and complexity of the English language.

    children). Its vocabulary is based on that of a parent language, although
    usually with significant pronunciation, meaning and grammar differences.
 5. Derivation :Derivation creates new words with different meanings, e.g.
    maltreat from treat. With different syntactic properties, e.g. the adverb quickly
    from the adjective quick.
 6. Diachronic linguistics : Diachronic linguistics (or historical linguistics), the
    study of a language over a period of time.
 7. Dialect : A dialect is a variety or version of a language spoken in a particular
    geographical area. Different dialects are distinguished from each other by
    their vocabulary, grammar and pronunciation (whereas a distinction made
    only in terms of pronunciation is usually called an accent). A dialect of a
    language is distinguishable, but still understandable, to speakers of another
    dialect of that language.
 8. Displacement : In linguistics, displacement is the capability of language to
    communicate about things that are not immediately present (spatially or
    temporally); i.e., things that are either not here or are not here now.

 9. Duality : Human language is organized at two levels or layers simultaneously.

    meaning. In a particular combination such as bin, we have another level

Lesson 01
                  INTRODUCTION TO LANGUAGE
Topic 001: What is Language?
What is language?

Answer: Language is a method of human communication, either spoken or written,
involving the use of words in a structured and conventional manner.

How is the term "language" used in various ways?

Answer: The term "language" is used in various ways, including as a set of words
and their pronunciation understood by a community, a means of communicating
ideas through signs, sounds, or gestures, and a formal system of signs and symbols.

What does "cultural transmission" mean in relation to language?
Answer: Cultural transmission refers to the process by which individuals acquire a
language within a particular culture, as opposed to inheriting it genetically.

Define language and explain its significance as a method of human
communication.

Answer: Language is a structured and conventional method of human
communication, involving the use of words either spoken or written. It serves as a
means of expression and understanding among communities. Language enables

 COMPILED BY SIR ZAHID                                                           1

individuals to convey ideas, thoughts, and feelings effectively, promoting social
interaction and cultural transmission.

Discuss the various ways in which the term "language" is defined and used.

Answer: The term "language" is defined in multiple ways:

According to Merriam-Webster, it's the words, pronunciation, and methods of
combining them understood by a community.

It's a systematic means of communicating using signs, sounds, gestures, or marks.
It includes formal systems of signs and symbols with rules for expression
transformation.

It refers to the form of verbal expression and specific style.

It encompasses vocabulary belonging to different arts or fields of knowledge.

It can also refer to specific words within laws or regulations.

Topic 002: Features of Language

What is displacement in language?
Answer: Displacement is the ability of language to discuss things beyond the
immediate present, such as times, places, and people not currently present.

What is arbitrariness in language?

Answer: Arbitrariness refers to the lack of inherent connection between a linguistic
form (word or symbol) and its meaning.

Explain the concept of productivity in language.

Answer: Productivity is the ability of language to create new expressions and novel
utterances, allowing for an infinite potential for communication.

Explain the concept of displacement in language and provide an example.

 COMPILED BY SIR ZAHID                                                            2

Answer: Displacement in language refers to the ability to communicate about times,
places, and people beyond the current context. An example is discussing a future
event or describing a location that is not physically present.

Describe the feature of arbitrariness in language and its implications.
Answer: Arbitrariness refers to the lack of inherent connection between linguistic
forms and their meanings. Words don't naturally resemble the objects or concepts
they represent. This feature emphasizes the cultural and conventional nature of
language, as different languages use different forms to represent the same concepts.

What is the concept of productivity in language, and why is it significant?
Answer: Productivity is the ability of language to generate new expressions and
novel utterances. This creative capacity allows humans to form an infinite number
of unique sentences and ideas using a finite set of linguistic elements. It enables
language to adapt to new situations and express complex thoughts.

Explain the role of cultural transmission in language acquisition.

Answer: Unlike physical traits, language isn't inherited. People acquire language
through exposure to their cultural environment. Language is passed down from one
generation to the next within a particular cultural context, allowing for the sharing
of knowledge and values.

Elaborate on the concept of duality in language structure.

Answer: Duality in language involves two simultaneous levels: the physical level of
producing individual sounds and the abstract level of creating sentences and
meanings. This dual nature enables humans to combine basic sounds into complex
structures to convey a wide range of ideas.

Topic 003: Elements that Make a Language

What is the most basic element of a natural language?

Answer: The most basic element of a natural language is its words.

How is grammar defined beyond just rules of structure and usage?

 COMPILED BY SIR ZAHID                                                            3

Answer: Grammar is seen as a way to describe recurring language patterns and how
these patterns function in different cultures and subcultures.

How does grammar help words in language?
Answer: Grammar dictates the order of words and introduces changes in their form
to provide temporal or relational information.

Describe the role of words in a language and how they convey meaning.

Answer: Words are fundamental elements of language that represent concepts. While
words may not directly resemble their meanings, their meanings are understood
through shared conventions. When words are used, they symbolize the concepts they
represent, facilitating communication between speakers.

Explain the evolving nature of grammar and its significance in language.

Answer: Grammar encompasses rules for word order and form that provide
additional context and meaning to words. It is more than just structure and usage; it
describes recurring language patterns and their functions in different cultures.
Grammar helps convey temporal and relational information within sentences.

ENG501
➡️ Introduction to Language

The study of language encompasses its structure, evolution, and usage. Language is a complex,
dynamic system of communication, consisting of sounds, words, and grammatical rules. It
shapes identity, culture, and society.

➡️ What do we Study in the History of a Language?

Language history examines the development, change, and spread of languages over time.
Scholars investigate linguistic evolution, influential events, and cultural interactions.

➡️ Basic Terms related to Language and Language History

Key terms include:

   -   Phonology (sound systems)
   -   Morphology (word formation)
   -   Syntax (sentence structure)
   -   Semantics (meaning)
   -   Lexicon (vocabulary)
   -   Dialectology (regional variations)
   -   Language families (genetic relationships)

➡️ Introduction to English Language

English, a Germanic language, originated in England and evolved through various stages. Its
global spread resulted from colonialism, trade, and technological advancements.

➡️ Importance of History of English Language

Understanding English language history provides insights into linguistic development, cultural
exchange, and literary evolution. It informs language teaching, linguistics research, and cultural
studies.

➡️ Historical Development of (English) Language and Related Terms

English language history spans:

   -    Old English (c. 450-1100)
   -    Middle English (c. 1100-1500)
   -    Early Modern English (c. 1500-1800)
   -    Modern English (c. 1800-present)

Key terms include:

   -    Germanic roots
   -    Norse and Norman influences
   -    Latin and Greek borrowings
   -    Colonial and global spread

➡️ Main Stages in the Development of English Language

   1.   Old English (Anglo-Saxon)
   2.   Middle English (Norman Conquest)
   3.   Early Modern English (Renaissance)
   4.   Modern English (Industrial Revolution)

➡️ Introduction to Old English: Birth of English- Prehistoric to Germanic History

Old English emerged from Germanic tribes' languages, influenced by Latin and Christianity. Key
features include:

   -    Inflectional grammar
   -    Complex syntax
   -    Limited vocabulary

➡️ Some Historical Facts about Old English

   -    Spoken by Anglo-Saxons (c. 450-1100)
   -    Influenced by Viking invasions
   -    Written records from 7th century

➡️ Features of Old English: Pronunciation and Vocabulary

   -    Phonetic spelling
   -    Inflectional endings
   -    Limited Latin borrowings
   -    Germanic vocabulary

➡️ The Grammar of Old English

   -    Case-based syntax
   -    Verbal conjugation

   -   Complex sentence structure

➡️ Discussion on Samples of Old English

Examples:

   -   Beowulf
   -   Caedmon's Hymn
   -   Anglo-Saxon Chronicle

➡️ Moving towards Middle English: The Norman Conquest (1066- 1200)

The Norman Conquest introduced French influences, transforming English language and culture.

➡️ The Re-establishment of English in Middle English Period

Middle English saw:

   -   Revival of English literature
   -   Emergence of vernacular language
   -   Influence of Latin and French

➡️ Middle English in 14th and 15th Centuries

Notable authors:

   -   Geoffrey Chaucer
   -   Sir Gawain and the Green Knight

➡️ Features of Middle English: Writing and Pronunciation

   -   Alphabetic script
   -   Vowel shifts
   -   French loanwords

Since importance of a language largely depends upon the importance of people who speak it;
with the rise of middle class English also had uplift in its status as their language.

   Q. English and England difference.

From the beginning, writers in the vernacular never called their language anything but Englisc
(English). The word is derived from the name of the Angles (OE Engle) but is used without
distinction for the language of all the invading tribes. From about the year 1000, the name
England (land of the Angles) began to be used in place of Angelcynn. The name English is thus
older than the name England.

Diachronic linguistics is the scientific study of language change over time. It’s also called
historical linguistics. Principal concerns include: to describe and account for observed changes
in particular languages. Diachronic linguistics is the study of language through different periods
in history. It maps the shifts, fractures, and mutations of languages over the centuries. In gross
outline, it is similar to evolutionary biology which maps the shifts and transformations of rocks.

Q: Explain Linguistics briefly.

A: The scientific study of language and its structure, including the study of
grammar, syntax, and phonetics. Specific branches of linguistics include

    ENG501 Midterm Short Notes BY PIN2 and MUHAMMAD (MAS All Rounder)

    ENG501 Midterm Short Notes BY PIN2 and MUHAMMAD (MAS All Rounder)

sociolinguistics, dialectology, psycholinguistics, computational linguistics,
comparative linguistics, and structural linguistics.

Q- Define diachronic linguistics.

A- Diachronic linguistics is the scientific study of language change over
time. It is the study of language through different periods in history. It maps
the shifts, fractures and mutations of languages over the centuries.

Q- Language of law court.

A- French was the language of lawyers and the law courts down to 1362.

Q- Difference between inflection and derivation?

A- Morphology has two main subdivisions, namely inflection and derivation.
Inflection deals with patterns of word structure that are determined by the
role of words in sentences. Derivation creates new words with different
meanings e.g., maltreat from treat.

Q- Role of literature in language.

A- Literature is a mirror of times and also a mirror of language/s used
during the times. So for example, literature written in England during the
Middle English period also reflects the times and language choices of the
times.

A- The terms Angli and Anglia occur beside Saxons and refer not to the
Angles individually but to the West Germanic tribes generally.

Q- Arbitrariness.

A- Arbitrariness: There is no ‘natural’ connection between a linguistic form
and its meaning.

Q- Time of old English.

A- c.500 to c.1100

    ENG501 Midterm Short Notes BY PIN2 and MUHAMMAD (MAS All Rounder)

A- The word ‘English’ is derived from the name of the Angles (OE Engle)
but is used without distinction for the language of all the invading tribes.

A- The definite article in ME is almost invariably ‘te’ or ‘the’.

A: In the fifteenth century, English succeeds in displacing Latin as the
general language spoken and written.

A: A language family is a group of languages related through descent from
a common ancestral language or parental language, called the
protolanguage of that family.

A: In the first decade of the fifteenth century, John Barton wrote a ‘Donet
François’, a treatise intended for adults who wished to learn French.

A: The Celtic languages in England had two divisions: Gaelic or Goidelic
branch and the Brythonic branch.

A: Control of the army and navy was in the hands of French people so
naturally French military terms were used. Examples include: army, navy,
peace, enemy, arms, battle, combat, skirmish, defense, ambush, retreat,
soldier, garrison, guard, and spy. Also Officers: captain, lieutenant and
sergeant are French words.

Q: Explain Linguistics briefly.

A: The scientific study of language and its structure, including the study of
grammar, syntax, and phonetics. Specific branches of linguistics include

sociolinguistics, dialectology, psycholinguistics, computational linguistics,
comparative linguistics, and structural linguistics.

Q- Define diachronic linguistics.

A- Diachronic linguistics is the scientific study of language change over
time. It is the study of language through different periods in history. It maps
the shifts, fractures and mutations of languages over the centuries.

Q- Language of law court.

A- French was the language of lawyers and the law courts down to 1362.

Q- Difference between inflection and derivation?

A- Morphology has two main subdivisions, namely inflection and derivation.
Inflection deals with patterns of word structure that are determined by the
role of words in sentences. Derivation creates new words with different
meanings e.g., maltreat from treat.

Q- Role of literature in language.

A- Literature is a mirror of times and also a mirror of language/s used
during the times. So for example, literature written in England during the
Middle English period also reflects the times and language choices of the
times.

Q- Anglicism. (*No such term found- Answer for the term ‘Anglia’)

A- The terms Angli and Anglia occur beside Saxons and refer not to the
Angles individually but to the West Germanic tribes generally.

Q- Arbitrariness.

A- Arbitrariness: There is no ‘natural’ connection between a linguistic form
and its meaning.

Q- Time of old English.

A- c.500 to c.1100

Q- Origin of word ‘English’.

A- The word ‘English’ is derived from the name of the Angles (OE Engle)
but is used without distinction for the language of all the invading tribes.

Q- Article in Middle English.

A- The definite article in ME is almost invariably ‘te’ or ‘the’.

Example: ‘te castles and bi the fet’.

Q: Status of Latin in 15th Century.

A: In the fifteenth century, English succeeds in displacing Latin as the
general language spoken and written.

Q: What is language family tree?
A: A language family is a group of languages related through descent from
a common ancestral language or parental language, called the
protolanguage of that family.

Q: What John Barton wrote in his book in 15th century?

A: In the first decade of the fifteenth century, John Barton wrote a ‘Donet
François’, a treatise intended for adults who wished to learn French.

Q: Two divisions in Celtic language.
A: The Celtic languages in England had two divisions: Gaelic or Goidelic
branch and the Brythonic branch.

Q: Army and Navy examples in Middle English.
A: Control of the army and navy was in the hands of French people so
naturally French military terms were used. Examples include: army, navy,
peace, enemy, arms, battle, combat, skirmish, defense, ambush, retreat,
soldier, garrison, guard, and spy. Also Officers: captain, lieutenant and
sergeant are French words.

Q: Difference between “Thee” and “Thou”.

A: Today we use you in both cases. In Old English, thou and thee were
singular and ye and you were plural, but in Middle English times the custom
arose of using ye/you as a polite or deferential way of addressing a single
person, and this usage spread; thou and thee gradually dropped out of use
in everyday speech, and finally disappeared (except in some dialects,
where they persist to this day).

Q6. Difference between inflection and derivation. 5 marks
Inflectional morphemes are affixes which carry grammatical meaning (for example, the plural -s in cats or progressive -ing in sailing). They do not change the part of speech or meaning of the word; they function to ensure that the word is in the appropriate form so the sentence is grammatically correct.
All inflectional morphemes in English are suffixes and are added after any derivational suffixes.
The most common inflectional morphemes are used in verb inflection (for example, -ed in raced, -ing in racing, -s in races) but there are suffixes for noun inflection (for example, plural -s in horses and possessive -'s in Norma's) and adjective inflection (for example, comparative -er in faster and superlative -est in fastest).
Derivational morphemes are affixes which are added to a lexeme to change its meaning or function. They are used to make a new, different lexeme (for example, -ly changes the adjective sad into the adverb sadly).
Most derivational morphemes change the part of speech, for example, -ance changes the verb resemble into the noun resemblance. Note that the 'e' is deleted at the end of the verb resemble when the suffix is added.

Question No: 17      ( Marks: 2 )
                                                                                         Writ
e down the partition process forBengal?

ANS: The Partition of Bengal in 1947 divided Bengal into the two separate entities
of West Bengal belonging to India, and East Bengal belonging to Pakistan. This was
part of the Partition of India and officially took place during August 14-August 15,
1947.East Bengal was renamed East Pakistan, and later became the independent
nation of Bangladeshafter the Bangladesh Liberation War of 1971.

Question No: 18      ( Marks: 2 )
                                                                                         Wh
at did Muslim gain from the Lucknow Pact?

ANS: The most significant achievement of this pact for the Muslims was that for the first
time the Congress had recognized the Muslim League as a representative body of the
Muslims of the sub-continent and they were granted separate electorates in the
provincial as well as in Imperial Legislative Council.

Question No: 19      ( Marks: 3 )
                                                                                         Writ
e a short note on The Quit India Movement 1942?

ANS: The Quit India Movement (Bharat Chhodo Andolan or the August
Movement) was a civil disobedience movement launched in India in August 1942 in
response to Mohandas Gandhi's call for immediate independence. Gandhi hoped to
bring the British government to the negotiating table. Almost the entire Indian National
Congress leadership, and not just at the national level, was put into confinement less
than twenty-four hours after Gandhi's speech, and the greater number of the Congress
leaders were to spend the rest of World War II in jail...

Question No: 20      ( Marks: 5 )
                                                                                         Exp
lain the Evolution of Two-Nation Theory in the Subcon?

ANS: The Two-Nation Theory was the basis for the Partition of India in 1947. It stated
that Muslims and Hindus were two separate nations by every definition, and therefore
Muslims should have an autonomous homeland in the Muslim majority areas ofBritish
India for the safeguard of their political, cultural, and social rights, within or without a
United India.

The Two-Nation Theory is the ideology that the primary identity of Muslims in
the Indiansubcontinent is their religion, rather than their language or ethnicity, and
therefore Indian Hindus and Muslims are two distinct nationalities, regardless of ethnic
or other commonalities.This Theory was a founding principle of the Pakistan
Movement (i.e. the Ideology of Pakistan), and the Partition of India in 1947.

at were Delhi Muslim Proposals? Discuss in detail.?

Important Muslim leaders on the initiative of the Quaid met in Delhi to discuss
constitutional and political issues. The major demands were:
_ Punjab and Bengal: statuary Muslim majorities
_ No Weightage in provinces
_ Sind to be separated from Bombay
_ Constitutional Reforms in NWFP
_ One-third seats for Muslims in Central Legislature
_ On communal issues, no law will be passed if three-fourth members of the
concerned community oppose it.
If these demands are accepted, they will give up ‘separate electorate.’ Subsequently,
the Muslim
League was divided in the Punjab, Shafi League and Jinnah League. Sir Muhammad
Shafi
opposed Jinnah on the issues:
_ Separate electorate
_ Attitude towards the Simon Commission. Jinnah continued his unremitting efforts
to promote Hindu-Muslim unity.

Question No: 17     ( Marks: 2 )
                                                                                     Writ
e a very short note on Pakistan National Movement in 1940?

 ANS: The Pakistan Movement refers to the independence movement
of Pakistanfrom the British Indian empire and its emergence as a sovereign country. It
has its origins in the United Provinces of Agra and Oudh. The movement was led by
lawyer Muhammad Ali Jinnah and such leaders as Allama Iqbal, Liaqat Ali Khan, Fatima
Jinnah,Bahadur Yar Jung, Maulana Mohammad Ali Jauhar, Huseyn Shaheed
Suhrawardy, A.K. Fazlul Huq, and Sardar Abdur Rab Nishtar, Sir Ziauddin Ahmed.

Question No: 19      ( Marks: 3 )
                                                                                    Wh
at were the main points of Lucknow Pact?

ANS: The main clauses of the Lucknow Pact were:
1. There shall be self-government in India.
2. Muslims should be given one-third representation in the central government
3. There should be separate electorates for all the communities until a community
demanded for joint electorates.
4. System of weightage should be adopted.

4. One third representation for Muslims in Central legislature
5. One fourth representation for Muslims in services
6. Sind to be made a province

Old English (450-1150 AD):
•      Old English, also known as Anglo-Saxon, was spoken from around the 5th century
       AD until the Norman Conquest in 1066.
•      It was heavily influenced by Germanic tribes, particularly the Angles, Saxons, and
       Jutes who invaded Britain.
•      Old English was characterized by a complex system of inflections and a
       vocabulary heavily rooted in Germanic languages.
•      Old English grammar was highly inflected, with nouns, pronouns, adjectives, and
       verbs changing form (inflecting) to indicate their grammatical function in a
       sentence.
•      Nouns had different forms based on case (nominative, accusative, genitive, and
       dative), number (singular and plural), and gender (masculine, feminine, and
       neuter).
•      Verbs had different forms based on tense (present, past, and past participle), mood
       (indicative, subjunctive, and imperative), person (first, second, and third), and
       number (singular and plural).
Middle English (1150-1500 AD):
       •       Following the Norman Conquest, Norman French became the language of
               the ruling elite, and Old English began to evolve into Middle English.
       •       During this period, English borrowed extensively from French, Latin, and
               other European languages.
       •       The Canterbury Tales by Geoffrey Chaucer, written in the late 14th
               century, is a prominent example of Middle English literature.
       •       Middle English saw a simplification of the inflectional system compared
               to Old English. Many inflectional endings were lost, and word order
               became more important for indicating grammatical relationships.
       •       Noun declensions were reduced, with fewer distinctions in case, gender,
               and number.
       •       The use of auxiliary verbs (e.g., "do," "will," "shall") began to emerge for
               expressing tense, mood, and aspect.

               •      Prepositions became more common for indicating relationships between
                      words in a sentence.
       Early Modern English (1500-1700 AD):
        •     The introduction of the printing press by William Caxton in 1476 and the
              standardization of English spelling by scholars like Samuel Johnson in the 18th
              century contributed to the stabilization of English.
        •     This period saw the Renaissance and the influx of Latin and Greek words into
              English, as well as the beginning of English exploration and colonization, which
              led to the incorporation of words from various languages worldwide.
        •     During the Early Modern English period, the grammar continued to evolve,
              influenced by developments such as the Renaissance and the standardization of
              English.
        •     The Great Vowel Shift, a significant sound change that affected the pronunciation
              of English vowels, occurred during this period but did not significantly impact
              grammar.
        •     The standardization of English spelling and grammar, particularly by scholars like
              William Shakespeare and Samuel Johnson, helped establish grammatical
              conventions that are still influential today.
       Modern English (1700 AD-present):
          •     Modern English continues to evolve, influenced by globalization, technology,
                and cultural exchange.
          •     The British Empire's expansion spread English around the world, resulting in
                diverse variations such as American English, Australian English, etc.
          •     In recent centuries, technological advancements, particularly in communication
                and transportation, have facilitated the rapid spread of English and the
                incorporation of new words, especially from fields like science and technology.
          •     Modern English grammar has continued to evolve, but the core grammatical
                structure remains largely consistent with Early Modern English.
          •     There have been changes in usage and style, influenced by factors such as
                technological advancements, globalization, and cultural shifts.
          •     Standard English grammar is taught and codified in grammar books,
                dictionaries, and style guides, but variation and flexibility in grammar are also
                recognized and accepted, especially in spoken language and informal writing.

Related terms in the study of the historical development of English include:
          Historical Linguistics: The study of how languages change over time.
          Philology: The study of language in written historical sources.
          Etymology: The study of the origin and history of words.
          Language Contact: The phenomenon where different languages come into contact and
          influence each other.

Lexicography: The practice of compiling dictionaries or the study of the vocabulary
of a language.
Standardization: The process by which a language or dialect becomes standardized,
usually through the development of grammatical rules and conventions.
Black Death: The Black Death was a deadly disease that spread across Europe in the
14th century. It was caused by a bacterium carried by fleas on rats. The disease killed
millions of people, leading to widespread fear and social and economic upheaval.

What is language?
Answer: Language is a method of human communication, either spoken or written,
involving the use of words in a structured and conventional manner.

How is the term "language" used in various ways?

Answer: The term "language" is used in various ways, including as a set of words
and their pronunciation understood by a community, a means of communicating
ideas through signs, sounds, or gestures, and a formal system of signs and symbols.

What does "cultural transmission" mean in relation to language?

Answer: Cultural transmission refers to the process by which individuals acquire a
language within a particular culture, as opposed to inheriting it genetically.

communication.

Answer: Language is a structured and conventional method of human
communication, involving the use of words either spoken or written. It serves as a
means of expression and understanding among communities. Language enables
individuals to convey ideas, thoughts, and feelings effectively, promoting social
interaction and cultural transmission.

Discuss the various ways in which the term "language" is defined and used.

Answer: The term "language" is defined in multiple ways:

According to Merriam-Webster, it's the words, pronunciation, and methods of
combining them understood by a community.

It's a systematic means of communicating using signs, sounds, gestures, or marks.

It includes formal systems of signs and symbols with rules for expression
transformation.

It refers to the form of verbal expression and specific style.

It encompasses vocabulary belonging to different arts or fields of knowledge.

It can also refer to specific words within laws or regulations.

Topic 002: Features of Language

What is displacement in language?
Answer: Displacement is the ability of language to discuss things beyond the
immediate present, such as times, places, and people not currently present.

What is arbitrariness in language?

Answer: Arbitrariness refers to the lack of inherent connection between a linguistic
form (word or symbol) and its meaning.

Explain the concept of productivity in language.

Answer: Productivity is the ability of language to create new expressions and novel
utterances, allowing for an infinite potential for communication.

places, and people beyond the current context. An example is discussing a future
event or describing a location that is not physically present.

Describe the feature of arbitrariness in language and its implications.
Answer: Arbitrariness refers to the lack of inherent connection between linguistic
forms and their meanings. Words don't naturally resemble the objects or concepts
they represent. This feature emphasizes the cultural and conventional nature of
language, as different languages use different forms to represent the same concepts.

What is the concept of productivity in language, and why is it significant?
Answer: Productivity is the ability of language to generate new expressions and
novel utterances. This creative capacity allows humans to form an infinite number
of unique sentences and ideas using a finite set of linguistic elements. It enables
language to adapt to new situations and express complex thoughts.

Explain the role of cultural transmission in language acquisition.

Answer: Unlike physical traits, language isn't inherited. People acquire language
through exposure to their cultural environment. Language is passed down from one
generation to the next within a particular cultural context, allowing for the sharing
of knowledge and values.

Elaborate on the concept of duality in language structure.

Answer: Duality in language involves two simultaneous levels: the physical level of
producing individual sounds and the abstract level of creating sentences and
meanings. This dual nature enables humans to combine basic sounds into complex
structures to convey a wide range of ideas.

Answer: The most basic element of a natural language is its words.

to provide temporal or relational information.

Topic 001: What is Language?
What is language?
Answer: Language is a method of human communication, either spoken or written,
involving the use of words in a structured and conventional manner.

How is the term "language" used in various ways?

Answer: The term "language" is used in various ways, including as a set of words
and their pronunciation understood by a community, a means of communicating
ideas through signs, sounds, or gestures, and a formal system of signs and symbols.

What does "cultural transmission" mean in relation to language?

Answer: Cultural transmission refers to the process by which individuals acquire a
language within a particular culture, as opposed to inheriting it genetically.
Define language and explain its significance as a method of human
communication.

 COMPILED BY SIRZAHID                                                            1

Answer: Language is a structured and conventional method of human
communication, involving the use of words either spoken or written. It serves as a
means of expression and understanding among communities. Language enables
individuals to convey ideas, thoughts, and feelings effectively, promoting social
interaction and cultural transmission.

Discuss the various ways in which the term "language" is defined and used.

Answer: The term "language" is defined in multiple ways:

According to Merriam-Webster, it's the words, pronunciation, and methods of
combining them understood by a community.

It's a systematic means of communicating using signs, sounds, gestures, or marks.

It includes formal systems of signs and symbols with rules for expression
transformation.

It refers to the form of verbal expression and specific style.

It encompasses vocabulary belonging to different arts or fields of knowledge.

It can also refer to specific words within laws or regulations.

Topic 002: Features of Language

What is displacement in language?
Answer: Displacement is the ability of language to discuss things beyond the
immediate present, such as times, places, and people not currently present.

What is arbitrariness in language?

Answer: Arbitrariness refers to the lack of inherent connection between a linguistic
form (word or symbol) and its meaning.

Explain the concept of productivity in language.

Answer: Productivity is the ability of language to create new expressions and novel
utterances, allowing for an infinite potential for communication.

Explain the concept of displacement in language and provide an example.

 COMPILED BY SIRZAHID                                                             2

Answer: Displacement in language refers to the ability to communicate about times,
places, and people beyond the current context. An example is discussing a future
event or describing a location that is not physically present.

Describe the feature of arbitrariness in language and its implications.
Answer: Arbitrariness refers to the lack of inherent connection between linguistic
forms and their meanings. Words don't naturally resemble the objects or concepts
they represent. This feature emphasizes the cultural and conventional nature of
language, as different languages use different forms to represent the same concepts.

What is the concept of productivity in language, and why is it significant?
Answer: Productivity is the ability of language to generate new expressions and
novel utterances. This creative capacity allows humans to form an infinite number
of unique sentences and ideas using a finite set of linguistic elements. It enables
language to adapt to new situations and express complex thoughts.

Explain the role of cultural transmission in language acquisition.

Answer: Unlike physical traits, language isn't inherited. People acquire language
through exposure to their cultural environment. Language is passed down from one
generation to the next within a particular cultural context, allowing for the sharing
of knowledge and values.

Elaborate on the concept of duality in language structure.

Answer: Duality in language involves two simultaneous levels: the physical level of
producing individual sounds and the abstract level of creating sentences and
meanings. This dual nature enables humans to combine basic sounds into complex
structures to convey a wide range of ideas.

Topic 003: Elements that Make a Language

What is the most basic element of a natural language?

Answer: The most basic element of a natural language is its words.

How is grammar defined beyond just rules of structure and usage?

 COMPILED BY SIRZAHID                                                             3

Answer: Grammar is seen as a way to describe recurring language patterns and how
these patterns function in different cultures and subcultures.

How does grammar help words in language?
Answer: Grammar dictates the order of words and introduces changes in their form
to provide temporal or relational information.

Describe the role of words in a language and how they convey meaning.

Answer: Words are fundamental elements of language that represent concepts. While
words may not directly resemble their meanings, their meanings are understood
through shared conventions. When words are used, they symbolize the concepts they
represent, facilitating communication between speakers.

Explain the evolving nature of grammar and its significance in language.

Answer: Grammar encompasses rules for word order and form that provide
additional context and meaning to words. It is more than just structure and usage; it
describes recurring language patterns and their functions in different cultures.
Grammar helps convey temporal and relational information within sentences.

How do speech and writing work together to convey information effectively?

Answer: Knowledge of words and grammar enables the creation of organized word

Lesson 31
  STANDARDIZATION OF ENGLISH IN THE 19TH AND
                20TH CENTURY
Topic 151: New Words in Modern English
What contributed to the immense increase in vocabulary items in the 19th and
20th century?

Scientists drew on various sources to form new vocabulary.

Give examples of words created by giving scientific meanings to existing ones.

Salt (chemistry), fruit and pollen (botany), parasite (zoology).

 COMPILED BY SIR ZAHID                                                      1

How were words borrowed from other languages to expand English
vocabulary?

Latin (bacillus, corolla), Greek (acne, eczema), German (cobalt, paraffin), and
names of European scientists.

What is a common way to create new words using Greek and Latin material?

Inventing them, e.g., biosphere, haemoglobin.

Explain the process of shortening words.
Shortened words often start as colloquial and may involve cutting off the beginning
or ending.

What is blending, and give examples of portmanteau words.

Blending combines words, e.g., brunch (breakfast + lunch); portmanteau words
include slithy and mimsy.

Topic 152: Standardization of Spelling & Changes in Pronunciation

How did printing contribute to the standardization of spelling?

Printing introduced widely accepted conventions, leading to standardized spelling in
printed books.
What were some differences in spelling between Addison's punctuation and
modern standards?

Minor differences like carry'd and publick.

Explain the changes in pronunciation during the Late Modern Period.
/r/ disappeared before consonants and a pause; pronunciation of certain words
changed.

What is a spelling pronunciation, and how does it arise?

Spelling pronunciation occurs when people learn words from print and may
mispronounce them based on their spelling.

 COMPILED BY SIR ZAHID                                                           2

Topic 153: Slang in the 19th and 20th Centuries

Define slang according to Webster in 1828.

"Low, vulgar, unmeaning language."

How did the definition of slang evolve according to the Oxford Dictionary
(1911)?

Language of a highly colloquial type, below the level of standard educated speech,
consisting of new or current words with special senses.
Provide examples of words that were once slang.

Boom, slump, crank, fad.

What role does slang play in language today?
Slang expresses a desire for freshness and novelty; it is more prevalent and
influential than in the past.

Topic 154: Issues of Register and Accent

What accent has been accepted as a standard in England for over a century?

RP (Received Pronunciation).

How has the prestige of accents changed in recent times?

RP has lost some prestige; regional accents, especially "soft" accents, are more
acceptable in many contexts.

Topic 155: British and Irish English

When did English rule extend over the entire island of Ireland?

16th–17th century.

How did Irish English originate?

In 1169 with competition between English, French, and Irish.

 COMPILED BY SIR ZAHID                                                         3

What impact did the loss of French have on the status of Irish and English in
Ireland?

Enhanced the status of Irish until the 17th century.

Describe a distinctive feature of Irish English pronunciation.

Use of spellings like tay (tea) and the influence of the Irish prepositional system.

How does Irish English differ syntactically from other dialects?
Irish dialects make more use of do-periphrasis, e.g., "They does be lonesome by
night."

Lesson 32
    19TH AND 20TH CENTURY ENGLISH: TENDENCIES
Topic 156: English Worldwide

What is the current status of English worldwide?

Answer: English is no longer exclusive to the British; it has global prevalence with
variations in former British Empire regions like the United States, Australia, Africa,
South Asia, and Canada.

Topic 157: Pidgins and Creoles

Define a pidgin and provide an example.

Answer: A pidgin is a simplified language used for trade between groups with no
common language. Example: Tok Pisin in Papua New Guinea.

When does a pidgin become a creole?

Answer: When a pidgin becomes the first language of a group, it transforms into a
creole.

Topic 158: The Oxford English Dictionary

 COMPILED BY SIR ZAHID                                                                 4

Why was The Oxford English Dictionary (OED) initiated?

Answer: The inadequacy of existing dictionaries led to the formation of a committee
in 1857 to create a comprehensive dictionary, recording words from around 1000
AD.

What were the two principal aims of The Oxford English Dictionary project?

Answer: To record every English word since 1000 AD and exhibit the history of each
word's forms, spellings, uses, and meanings.

Topic 159: Grammatical Tendencies - Verb-Adverb Combinations

Explain the development of the get passive in the 19th century.

Answer: The get passive (e.g., 'he got hurt') emerged in the 19th century for dynamic
expression compared to 'he is hurt' or 'he became hurt.'

What is a significant tendency related to verb-adverb combinations in modern
English?

Answer: The extension of verb-adverb combinations, often one-syllable verbs with
adverbs, shows figurative and idiomatic usage.

Topic 160: Summary of Characteristics of the 19th and 20th Century English

How did the 19th and 20th centuries view linguistic questions differently?
Answer: They adopted a more enlightened and tolerant approach, accepting
colloquial and regional forms.
What were the main influences on vocabulary changes during the 19th and 20th
centuries?
Answer: Changes were driven by the influence of science, media, and technology,
while grammar remained relatively stable.

Topic 091: Middle English Syntax

What resulted in the leveling of inflections in Middle English?

Leveling of inflections resulted in syntactic and semantic relationships that had been
signaled by the endings on words.
How did Old English and Middle English differ in expressing grammatical
functions of consecutive nouns?

In Old English, grammatical functions were clear from the endings, while in Middle
English, their functions might become uncertain.

What was the most direct way to avoid ambiguity in Middle English syntax?

The most direct way was through limiting the possible patterns of word order.

Describe the shift observed in Middle English syntax.

 COMPILED BY SIR ZAHID                                                             1

There was a shift from a highly synthetic stage in Old English to the highly analytic
stages of Late Middle English and Modern English.

What period does the Peterborough Chronicle span, and what changes can be
traced in its text?
The Peterborough Chronicle spans from 1070 to 1154, and it shows a significant loss
of inflections followed by a corresponding rigidity of word order.

Topic 092: Middle English Vocabulary

What influenced the loss of inflections and simplification of grammar in Middle
English vocabulary?

The loss of inflections and simplification of grammar was influenced directly by the
use of French.

What aspects are significant in understanding the nature of the interchange of
words between French and English?

Mutual & frequent, no sudden change, varying tempo, and a slow beginning.

Give examples of French words influencing fashion and social life in Middle
English.

Examples include fashion, dress, apparel, gown, robe, garment, and others.
Which areas of life in Middle English were influenced by French words related
to government and administration?

Words such as government, crown, state, empire, parliament, and titles of offices
like chancellor and treasurer.

What were some Middle English words borrowed from French related to law
and the military?
Legal terms: felony, trespass, assault; Military terms: army, navy, battle, captain,
lieutenant.

Topic 093: Borrowings in Middle English

 COMPILED BY SIR ZAHID                                                            2

How did literature contribute to the entrance of French words into Middle
English?

Literature was a channel for the entrance of French words, and Middle English
literature was based directly on French originals.

How did Latin borrowings differ from French borrowings in Middle English?

Latin borrowings were less popular and generally entered through the written
language, often through literature.

Topic 094: The Rise of Standard English
Which dialect contributed the most to the formation of standard written
English?

The East Midland dialect contributed the most.

What were some characteristics of the East Midland dialect that made it a basis
for standardization?

It represented a compromise in sounds and inflections, and it was less conservative
than the Southern dialect and less radical than the Northern.

What role did the universities, Oxford and Cambridge, play in the rise of
Standard English?
The presence of universities in the East Midland region, particularly Oxford and
Cambridge, contributed to its intellectual development.

Topic 095: Importance of London Standard

Why was London significant in the rise of Standard English?
London was the political capital, commercial center, seat of judicial tribunals, and a
focus of social and intellectual activities in England.

How did London's economy contribute to the spread of Standard English?

London's economy served as an "engine of communication and exchange,"
facilitating the distribution of ideas and information.

 COMPILED BY SIR ZAHID                                                             3

What factors made London English influential, and what was the influence
reciprocal?

London's status as a political and economic hub made its English influential, and the
influence was reciprocal as people took back forms and usages from the city.

What significant event in 1476 contributed to the spread of London English?

The introduction of printing in 1476 played a crucial role in the dissemination of
London English, with Caxton using the current speech of London.

By when had the London standard been accepted in most parts of the country,
and what was a key reason for this acceptance?

In the latter part of the fifteenth century, the London standard had been accepted, at
least in writing, with the introduction of printing being a key reason.

              has since been “nativized” (i.e. taught to, and acquired by, children). Its
              vocabulary is based on that of a parent language, although usually with significant
              pronunciation, meaning and grammar differences.

Derivation : Derivation creates new words with different meanings, e.g. maltreat from treat.
             With different syntactic properties, e.g. the adverb quickly from the adjective
             quick.

Diachronic Diachronic linguistics (or historical linguistics), the study of a language over a
linguistics : period of time.

Dialect :     A dialect is a variety or version of a language spoken in a particular geographical
              area. Different dialects are distinguished from each other by their vocabulary,
              grammar and pronunciation (whereas a distinction made only in terms of
              pronunciation is usually called an accent). A dialect of a language is
              distinguishable, but still understandable, to speakers of another dialect of that
              language.

Displacement In linguistics, displacement is the capability of language to communicate about
:            things that are not immediately present (spatially or temporally); i.e., things that
             are either not here or are not here now.

Duality :     Human language is organized at two levels or layers simultaneously. We have a
              physical level at which we can produce individual sounds, like n, b and i. As
              individual sounds, none of these discrete forms has any intrinsic meaning. In a

               particular combination such as bin, we have another level producing a meaning
               that is different from the meaning of the combination in nib.Among other
               creatures, each communicative signal appears to be a single fixed form that cannot
               be broken down into separate parts.Your dog may be able to produce woof (“I’m
               happy to see you”).It does not seem to do so on the basis of a distinct level of
               production combining the separate elements of w+oo+f. If the dog was operating
               with the double level (i.e. duality), then we might expect to hear different
               combinations with different meanings, such as oowf (“I’m hungry”) and foow
               (“I’m really bored”).

Englishes :    World English is one language and Englishes are different variety of English like
               Austrian English, American English and South Asian English (Indian English,
               Pakistan English etc.)

               words in sentences. For example, a pronoun like he has the forms he, him and his
               depending on whether it is subject, object or possessive in a given sentence.

Juncture :     The pauses or connections between words, phrases, and sentences.

Q. Varieties of English in South Asia
 • Bangladeshi English
 • Indian English
 • Nepali English
 • Pakistani English
 • Sri Lankan English
 Q. Spread of English in South Asia?
 The worldwide spread of English is an unprecedented phenomenon for which we do not find any example in
 human history. English was brought to the subcontinent in the early seventeenth century by British colonialism.
 Today, it is spoken as a second language by 3 percent of the population of Bangladesh, Bhutan, India, the
 Maldives, Nepal, Pakistan, and Sri Lanka. In numerical terms, we can safely say that there are approximately 33
 million English speaking people.
 South Asian English is sometimes called ‘Indian English’ as British India included most of the region, but
 today, the varieties of English are usually divided according to the modern states. In India, there are 25 million
 users of English, even more than Australia. There are intra-national and intra-regional role of ‘link’ language
 among people of diverse linguistic backgrounds. After so many years of independence, the countries of South
 Asia still use English to varying degrees in the domains of government administration, law, the military, higher
 education, commerce, the media, and the arts.
 In Pakistan, English has the status of an official language alongside the national language, Urdu. In Sri Lanka,
 there are efforts to ‘peoplize’ English. In Bangladesh, despite strong Bangla movement, English enjoys
 importance. In South Asian countries, it plays the role of the international medium for communication with the
 global community of nations.
 Q. Features of South Asian English
 Indian English
 It has words of Indian vernaculars that have made their way into the English language.
 Examples include jungle, tank, bungalow, shampoo, verandah.
 It has political, sociological, and administrative terms of modern India: dharna, hartal, eveteasing, votebank,
 swdeshi, tiffin, hillstation, gymkhana. We need to notice its resemblance with Pakistani English.
 Vocabulary
 •      Our company lays great stress on technical training and knowledge ‘upgradation’.
 •      The Prime Minister greeted the presspersons with a ‘namaskar’ and a broad smile.
 •      I read the newspaper ‘matrimonials’ on Sundays, especially the ‘English-knowing’ intelligentsia.
 Spelling and Pronunciation
 Most Indian languages, unlike English, have a nearly phonetic spelling, so the spelling of a word is a highly
 reliable guide to its pronunciation. The word ‘of’ is usually pronounced with a /f/ instead of a /v/ as in most

other accents. Pronunciation of <house> as [hauz] is prevalent for both noun and verb instead of [haus] as noun
and [hauz] as verb.
